Sun.explanation: The Sun contains 99.8% of all the mass in our solar system
points: The Sun is a G2V main-sequence star with a diameter of about 1.39 million kilometers and a surface temperature of roughly 5,500 °C.
It generates energy through nuclear fusion in its core, converting about 4 million tons of hydrogen into helium every second.
The Sun's mass is 333,000 times that of Earth, making it the dominant gravitational body in the solar system.
Its outer atmosphere, the corona, reaches millions of degrees Celsius and produces the solar wind that shapes planetary magnetospheres.
The Sun has an 11-year activity cycle with varying sunspots, flares, and coronal mass ejections that affect Earth's climate and technology.

Sirius.explanation: Sirius is the brightest star in Earth's night sky and is twice the size of our Sun
points: Sirius is a binary system consisting of Sirius A (a main-sequence star of spectral type A1V) and the faint white dwarf Sirius B.
Sirius A is about 25 times more luminous than the Sun and has a surface temperature of around 9,940 K, giving it a brilliant white-blue color.
At a distance of 8.6 light-years, it is one of the closest bright stars to Earth and appears brightest due to its proximity and high intrinsic luminosity.
Sirius B is a white dwarf with roughly the mass of the Sun compressed into a volume similar to Earth's, making it extremely dense.
The system has a 50-year orbital period, and Sirius was known to ancient civilizations as the 'Dog Star' associated with the Nile flooding and summer heat.

Alpha Centauri.explanation: Alpha Centauri is the nearest star system to Earth at just 4.37 light-years away
points: Alpha Centauri is a triple-star system consisting of Alpha Centauri A (G2V, Sun-like), Alpha Centauri B (K1V, orange dwarf), and Proxima Centauri (M5.5Ve red dwarf).
Alpha Centauri A and B form a binary pair orbiting each other every 80 years, while Proxima orbits the pair at a much greater distance.
Proxima Centauri, at 4.24 light-years, is the closest known star to the Sun and hosts at least one confirmed planet (Proxima b) in the habitable zone.
Alpha Centauri A is very similar to the Sun in mass, size, and luminosity, making it a prime target for future interstellar exploration.
The system is moving toward the Sun and will reach its closest approach in about 28,000 years at roughly 3 light-years distance.

Proxima Centauri.explanation: Proxima Centauri is the single closest known star to our Sun at 4.24 light-years
points: Proxima Centauri is a small red dwarf (M5.5Ve) with only 12% of the Sun's mass and 0.0017% of its luminosity.
It is gravitationally bound to the Alpha Centauri A/B binary but orbits at about 0.21 light-years from them.
Proxima b, discovered in 2016, is an Earth-mass planet in the habitable zone, though it faces intense stellar flares.
Proxima experiences frequent flares that can increase its brightness dramatically and strip atmospheres from nearby planets.
It is the nearest star system and a primary target for future interstellar probes like Breakthrough Starshot.

Betelgeuse.explanation: Betelgeuse is a massive red supergiant star that will explode as a supernova one day
points: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant of spectral type M1-2Ia-Ib located in the constellation Orion, about 640 light-years from Earth.
It has a radius approximately 600–1,000 times that of the Sun and is one of the largest known stars visible to the naked eye.
Betelgeuse is highly variable in brightness due to pulsations and mass loss, and it dimmed dramatically in 2019–2020 (the 'Great Dimming').
It is expected to explode as a Type II supernova within the next 100,000 years, potentially becoming as bright as a full Moon for weeks.
The star has already lost much of its outer envelope and is in its final evolutionary stages before core collapse.

Rigel.explanation: Rigel is a blue supergiant star 120,000 times more luminous than our Sun
points: Rigel is a blue supergiant of spectral type B8 Ia located in Orion, approximately 860 light-years from Earth.
It has a surface temperature of about 12,100 K and is one of the most intrinsically luminous stars visible in the night sky.
Rigel is a multiple star system with at least four components, though Rigel A dominates the visible light.
It is losing mass rapidly through a strong stellar wind and is expected to end its life as a supernova in the relatively near future (astronomically speaking).
Rigel appears as the brightest star in Orion after Betelgeuse during certain periods due to variability in both stars.

Vega.explanation: Vega will become Earth's pole star in about 13,000 years due to axial precession
points: Vega is an A0V main-sequence star located 25 light-years away in the constellation Lyra.
It is one of the brightest stars in the northern sky and has a very high rotational velocity, causing it to bulge at the equator.
Vega is surrounded by a prominent debris disk of dust and is the prototype for 'Vega-type' systems.
Due to Earth's axial precession, Vega will be the northern pole star around the year 14,000 CE.
It serves as a standard star for calibrating astronomical brightness and is one of the most studied stars in the sky.

Polaris.explanation: Polaris is the North Star that always points north and barely moves in the night sky
points: Polaris (Alpha Ursae Minoris) is a yellow supergiant (F7 Ib) located about 430 light-years away.
It is very close to the north celestial pole (currently within 0.7°), making it appear nearly stationary while other stars circle around it.
Polaris is actually a triple star system, with Polaris A being a Cepheid variable that pulsates every 4 days.
It has been used for navigation for centuries and is currently the most useful pole star.
Due to precession, Polaris will gradually move away from the pole over the next few thousand years.

Canopus.explanation: Canopus is the second brightest star in the sky and is used to navigate spacecraft
points: Canopus (Alpha Carinae) is a yellow-white supergiant (F0 II) located about 310 light-years away.
It is intrinsically one of the most luminous stars visible from Earth, about 10,000–15,000 times brighter than the Sun.
Canopus is too far south to be visible from most northern latitudes but is prominent in the southern hemisphere.
It has been used as a reference star for spacecraft navigation due to its brightness and stable position.
Canopus is nearing the end of its life and will eventually explode as a supernova.

Arcturus.explanation: Arcturus is the brightest star in the northern sky and a bright orange-red giant
points: Arcturus (Alpha Boötis) is an orange giant star (K0 III) located about 37 light-years from Earth.
It is roughly 25 times the diameter of the Sun and 170 times more luminous.
Arcturus is relatively old and has exhausted hydrogen in its core, now fusing helium.
It has a high proper motion and is part of the Arcturus moving group of stars.
Arcturus is easy to find by following the arc of the Big Dipper's handle ('arc to Arcturus').

Aldebaran.explanation: Aldebaran is a giant orange star 44 times the diameter of our Sun
points: Aldebaran (Alpha Tauri) is a red giant (K5 III) located about 65 light-years away in the constellation Taurus.
It has a diameter about 44 times that of the Sun and is 425 times more luminous.
Aldebaran appears to be the 'eye' of Taurus the Bull and has a faint companion star.
It is losing mass through a stellar wind and is in a late stage of stellar evolution.
Aldebaran is one of the brightest stars in the winter sky and easily visible to the naked eye.

Antares.explanation: Antares is a red supergiant so massive that if placed where our Sun is it would reach beyond Mars
points: Antares (Alpha Scorpii) is a red supergiant (M1.5 Iab) located about 550 light-years away in Scorpius.
Its radius is estimated at 680–800 times that of the Sun, making it one of the largest known stars.
Antares is a binary system with a hot blue companion star orbiting it.
It is highly luminous (about 10,000–12,000 times the Sun) and is losing mass rapidly.
Antares is expected to explode as a supernova in the next million years or so.

Spica.explanation: Spica is a binary star system and one of the bluest and hottest visible stars
points: Spica (Alpha Virginis) is a binary system consisting of two B-type main-sequence stars located about 250 light-years away.
The primary star is a B1 III-IV star with a surface temperature of about 25,000 K.
The system is an eclipsing binary with a short orbital period of about 4 days.
Spica is one of the brightest stars in the northern sky and appears very blue-white.
It is used as a standard star for calibrating astronomical observations.

Capella.explanation: Capella is actually four stars in two binary pairs all orbiting together
points: Capella (Alpha Aurigae) is a quadruple star system located about 42 light-years away.
It consists of two yellow giant stars (Capella Aa and Ab) in a close binary orbit, plus two distant red dwarfs.
The two giants are about 9–10 times the Sun's radius and are in a 104-day orbit.
Capella appears as the brightest star in the constellation Auriga and one of the brightest in the northern sky.
The system is a spectroscopic binary, meaning its components are only separable through spectroscopy.

Deneb.explanation: Deneb is so luminous it would outshine a crescent Moon if it were as close as Sirius
points: Deneb (Alpha Cygni) is a blue-white supergiant (A2 Ia) located about 2,600 light-years away in Cygnus.
It is one of the most luminous stars known, with an intrinsic brightness of about 200,000 times the Sun.
Deneb is part of the Summer Triangle asterism along with Vega and Altair.
It is losing mass through a strong stellar wind and is in a late evolutionary stage.
Deneb is expected to explode as a supernova in the future.

Fomalhaut.explanation: Fomalhaut has a wide debris disk surrounding it with possible young planets forming
points: Fomalhaut (Alpha Piscis Austrini) is an A3V main-sequence star located about 25 light-years away.
It is surrounded by a prominent debris disk visible in infrared light.
A planet candidate (Fomalhaut b) was imaged but later found to be a dust cloud.
Fomalhaut is one of the closest stars with a visible debris disk, similar to the Kuiper Belt.
It is relatively young (about 440 million years old) and still has planet-forming material around it.

Regulus.explanation: Regulus is a rapidly spinning star that bulges at its equator from its fast rotation
points: Regulus (Alpha Leonis) is a multiple star system located about 79 light-years away in Leo.
The primary star (Regulus A) is a blue-white main-sequence star (B7V) spinning extremely rapidly.
Its equatorial radius is about 32% larger than its polar radius due to centrifugal forces.
Regulus is part of a quadruple system with three other faint companions.
It is one of the brightest stars in the constellation Leo and easy to spot in spring skies.

Castor.explanation: Castor is a remarkable sextuple star system of six stars all bound together
points: Castor (Alpha Geminorum) is a six-star system located about 51 light-years away in Gemini.
It consists of three binary pairs: two A-type main-sequence stars and one faint red dwarf pair.
The components orbit each other in hierarchical orbits with periods from hours to thousands of years.
Castor appears as a single bright star to the naked eye but is easily resolved with telescopes.
It is one of the most complex multiple star systems visible to amateur astronomers.

Pollux.explanation: Pollux is a giant orange star with a confirmed planet orbiting it
points: Pollux (Beta Geminorum) is an orange giant star (K0 III) located about 34 light-years away.
It is about 8 times the Sun's radius and 33 times more luminous.
Pollux has a confirmed exoplanet (Pollux b), a gas giant with about 2.9 Jupiter masses.
The planet orbits at about 1.7 AU with a period of 590 days.
Pollux is one of the brightest stars in Gemini and marks the head of the constellation.

Procyon.explanation: Procyon is a binary star that has a faint white dwarf companion orbiting it
points: Procyon (Alpha Canis Minoris) is a binary system located about 11.5 light-years away.
The primary is a yellow-white main-sequence star (F5 IV-V) about 7 times more luminous than the Sun.
Procyon B is a white dwarf with roughly the mass of the Sun but the size of Earth.
The two stars orbit each other every 40 years.
Procyon is the brightest star in Canis Minor and one of the closest bright stars to Earth.

Epsilon Eridani.explanation: Epsilon Eridani is a young star similar to our young Sun and has a confirmed planet
points: Epsilon Eridani is a K2V orange dwarf located about 10.5 light-years away.
It is relatively young (about 800 million years old) and has a prominent debris disk.
A confirmed planet (ε Eri b) is a gas giant orbiting at about 3.4 AU.
The star has been extensively studied as a nearby analog to the early Sun.
It is one of the closest stars with a confirmed planet and a debris disk.

Tau Ceti.explanation: Tau Ceti is one of the most Sun-like stars visible to the naked eye
points: Tau Ceti (52 Ceti) is a G8.5V main-sequence star located about 11.9 light-years away.
It is very similar to the Sun in mass, size, and temperature but slightly less luminous.
Tau Ceti has been a prime target for SETI searches due to its stability and similarity to the Sun.
Multiple planet candidates have been proposed, though none are confirmed.
It is one of the closest single Sun-like stars to Earth.

Barnard's Star.explanation: Barnard's Star has the fastest proper motion across the sky of any known star
points: Barnard's Star is a red dwarf (M4V) located about 6 light-years away.
It has the largest proper motion of any star (10.3 arcseconds per year).
A super-Earth planet candidate (Barnard's Star b) was announced but later disputed.
It is one of the closest stars to the Sun and the closest solitary red dwarf.
Its high velocity suggests it may be an older star passing through our neighborhood.

Wolf 359.explanation: Wolf 359 is one of the faintest and smallest known red dwarf stars near the Sun
points: Wolf 359 is an M6V red dwarf located about 7.9 light-years away.
It is extremely faint (absolute magnitude ~16.6) and only about 10% the mass of the Sun.
It is known for frequent flares that can temporarily increase its brightness.
Wolf 359 was the fictional home system of the Enterprise in Star Trek.
It is one of the closest stars to Earth and a typical example of a very low-mass red dwarf.

Luyten's Star.explanation: Luyten's Star is a red dwarf with a potentially habitable planet in a close orbit
points: Luyten's Star (GJ 273) is an M3.5V red dwarf located about 12.4 light-years away.
It hosts a super-Earth planet (Luyten b) in the habitable zone.
The planet receives about the same stellar flux as Earth from the Sun.
Luyten's Star is relatively quiet for a red dwarf, reducing atmospheric stripping risk.
It was one of the targets for Breakthrough Listen SETI searches.

Ross 128.explanation: Ross 128 is one of the quietest red dwarfs making its planet more habitable
points: Ross 128 is an M4V red dwarf located about 11 light-years away.
It hosts a temperate super-Earth (Ross 128 b) in the habitable zone.
The star is unusually quiet for a red dwarf, with few flares.
The planet may have conditions suitable for liquid water.
It is one of the closest potentially habitable exoplanet systems.

TRAPPIST-1.explanation: TRAPPIST-1 is an ultra-cool red dwarf hosting seven rocky planets including habitable zone ones
points: TRAPPIST-1 is an M8V ultra-cool dwarf located about 40 light-years away.
It hosts seven Earth-sized planets, three in the habitable zone.
All planets are likely tidally locked and orbit very close to their star.
The system is ideal for studying multi-planet atmospheres and habitability.
TRAPPIST-1 planets are among the most promising targets for JWST observations.

Gliese 667C.explanation: Gliese 667C hosts multiple potentially habitable super-Earth planets around it
points: Gliese 667C is an M3V red dwarf component of a triple star system, about 23 light-years away.
It hosts at least two super-Earth planets (Gliese 667Cc and Ce) in the habitable zone.
Gliese 667Cc receives about 90% of Earth's insolation.
The star is part of a triple system, which may affect planetary stability.
It was one of the first systems with multiple habitable-zone planets.

Kepler-452.explanation: Kepler-452 is very similar to our Sun and hosts a planet often called Earth's older cousin
points: Kepler-452 is a G2-type star very similar to the Sun, located about 1,800 light-years away.
It hosts Kepler-452b, a super-Earth orbiting in the habitable zone.
The planet is about 60% larger than Earth and has been in the habitable zone longer than Earth.
The star is about 1.5 billion years older than the Sun.
Kepler-452b is one of the most Earth-like planets discovered by the Kepler mission.

55 Cancri A.explanation: 55 Cancri A hosts five known planets including one giant in a wide orbit
points: 55 Cancri A is a Sun-like G8V star located about 41 light-years away.
It hosts a system of five planets, including 55 Cancri e (a super-Earth) and a gas giant.
55 Cancri e is one of the first discovered hot super-Earths.
The system is relatively close and bright, making it good for follow-up observations.
The outer planet has a long orbital period of about 14 years.

HR 8799.explanation: HR 8799 is a young star with four directly imaged gas giant planets around it
points: HR 8799 is an A5V star located about 130 light-years away.
It hosts four massive gas giant planets directly imaged by telescopes.
The planets orbit at very wide distances (14–68 AU).
The system is young (about 30 million years old) and provides a snapshot of planet formation.
It is one of the few systems with directly imaged exoplanets.

Beta Pictoris.explanation: Beta Pictoris is surrounded by a huge dusty disk and has a planet already photographed
points: Beta Pictoris is an A6V star located about 63 light-years away.
It has a prominent edge-on debris disk visible in scattered light.
Beta Pictoris b is a directly imaged gas giant planet orbiting at about 9 AU.
The system is young (about 20 million years old) and actively forming planets.
It is one of the best-studied young planetary systems.

Eta Carinae.explanation: Eta Carinae is one of the most massive stars known and will soon become a hypernova
points: Eta Carinae is a massive binary system located about 7,500 light-years away in the Carina Nebula.
The primary star has a mass estimated at 100–150 solar masses.
It underwent a great eruption in the 1840s, temporarily becoming the second brightest star in the sky.
The system is surrounded by the Homunculus Nebula from the eruption.
It is expected to explode as a hypernova or pair-instability supernova within the next few hundred thousand years.

VY Canis Majoris.explanation: VY Canis Majoris is one of the largest known stars so big that light takes hours to cross it
points: VY Canis Majoris is a red hypergiant located about 3,900 light-years away.
Its radius is estimated at 1,400–2,000 times that of the Sun.
It is extremely luminous (about 270,000 times the Sun) but obscured by dust.
The star is losing mass rapidly and is in its final evolutionary stages.
If placed at the Sun's position, its surface would extend beyond Saturn.

UY Scuti.explanation: UY Scuti is one of the largest known stars with a radius over 1,700 times that of the Sun
points: UY Scuti is a red supergiant located about 9,500 light-years away in Scutum.
Its radius is estimated at 1,700–2,000 solar radii.
It is highly variable and obscured by dust.
The star is losing mass rapidly through powerful stellar winds.
If placed at the Sun's position, its surface would extend beyond Jupiter.

Stephenson 2-18.explanation: Stephenson 2-18 is potentially the largest known star with a radius 2,150 times the Sun
points: Stephenson 2-18 is a red supergiant in the open cluster Stephenson 2.
Its radius is estimated at around 2,150 solar radii (though with large uncertainty).
It is extremely luminous but heavily obscured by interstellar dust.
The star is in a very late evolutionary stage and losing mass rapidly.
Size estimates for such stars have significant uncertainties due to distance and dust.

R136a1.explanation: R136a1 is the most massive known star at around 200 solar masses in the Milky Way
points: R136a1 is a Wolf-Rayet star located in the R136 cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud.
It has a current mass of about 200 solar masses (originally ~315 solar masses).
It is extremely luminous (about 8.7 million times the Sun) and hot (surface temperature ~53,000 K).
R136a1 is losing mass at an enormous rate through powerful stellar winds.
It is expected to end its life as a pair-instability supernova or black hole.

Pistol Star.explanation: The Pistol Star is one of the most luminous stars known near the Milky Way's center
points: The Pistol Star is a luminous blue variable located about 25,000 light-years away in the galactic center.
It has a luminosity of about 3.3 million times the Sun.
It is heavily obscured by dust and only visible in infrared.
The star is surrounded by the Pistol Nebula from its mass loss.
It is one of the most massive and luminous stars in the Milky Way.

Peony Star.explanation: The Peony Star near the galactic center may be even more luminous than the Pistol Star
points: The Peony Star (WR 102ka) is a Wolf-Rayet star in the galactic center region.
Its luminosity is estimated at around 5 million times the Sun.
It is heavily obscured and only observable in infrared.
The star is losing mass rapidly and surrounded by a nebula.
It is one of the most extreme stars known in our galaxy.

LBV 1806-20.explanation: LBV 1806-20 is an extremely luminous hypergiant star close to the Milky Way's core
points: LBV 1806-20 is a luminous blue variable located about 28,000 light-years away.
It has a luminosity of about 2–5 million times the Sun.
It is associated with a magnetar (SGR 1806-20) and a massive star cluster.
The star is extremely massive and variable.
It is one of the most luminous stars in the Milky Way.

Zeta Puppis.explanation: Zeta Puppis is a hot luminous blue supergiant shedding mass in powerful stellar winds
points: Zeta Puppis (Naos) is an O4 If(n) supergiant located about 1,080 light-years away.
It has a surface temperature of about 40,000 K and is 800,000 times more luminous than the Sun.
The star has powerful stellar winds moving at over 2,500 km/s.
It is rapidly rotating and has a bow shock visible in ultraviolet.
Zeta Puppis is one of the brightest O-type stars visible from Earth.

P Cygni.explanation: P Cygni is a luminous blue variable that brightened dramatically in the year 1600
points: P Cygni is a luminous blue variable (B1 Ia+) located about 5,000–7,000 light-years away.
It underwent a major eruption in 1600, increasing in brightness significantly.
The star is losing mass through strong stellar winds and is surrounded by shells.
It is one of the prototypes of the LBV class.
P Cygni profiles in spectral lines are named after this star.

Rho Cassiopeiae.explanation: Rho Cassiopeiae is a yellow hypergiant one of the rarest types of stars in existence
points: Rho Cassiopeiae is a yellow hypergiant (F8-G2 Ia0) located about 3,400 light-years away.
It is one of the most luminous stars in the Milky Way (about 500,000 times the Sun).
The star undergoes rare outbursts when it ejects outer layers.
It is extremely rare and unstable, in a brief evolutionary phase.
Rho Cas is one of the few known yellow hypergiants.

HR Carinae.explanation: HR Carinae is a luminous blue variable periodically undergoing violent eruptions
points: HR Carinae is an LBV located about 16,000 light-years away.
It has a luminosity of about 500,000 times the Sun.
The star has shown multiple eruptions and mass-loss episodes.
It is surrounded by a nebula from ejected material.
HR Car is one of the southern hemisphere's most studied LBVs.

W Virginis.explanation: W Virginis is a type II Cepheid variable star pulsating in size and brightness
points: W Virginis is the prototype of Type II Cepheids (population II Cepheids).
It pulsates with a period of about 17 days.
These stars are older, metal-poor Cepheids found in globular clusters.
They are used as distance indicators in some contexts.
W Vir variables bridge classical Cepheids and RR Lyrae stars.

Mira.explanation: Mira is a pulsating variable star that changes from barely visible to very bright
points: Mira (Omicron Ceti) is a red giant and the prototype of Mira-type long-period variables.
It pulsates with a period of about 332 days, changing brightness by a factor of 1,500.
Mira is losing mass through a strong stellar wind, creating a tail visible in ultraviolet.
It has a white dwarf companion that interacts with its wind.
Mira was the first non-supernova variable star discovered (1596).

Chi Cygni.explanation: Chi Cygni is a Mira-type variable that grows to over 400 times the Sun's size
points: Chi Cygni is a long-period variable with a period of about 408 days.
At maximum, it expands to over 400 solar radii.
It varies from magnitude +3.3 to +14.2.
Chi Cyg is one of the largest known periodic variable stars.
It is a typical late-stage red giant losing mass rapidly.

RR Lyrae.explanation: RR Lyrae variables are used as distance markers across the Milky Way galaxy
points: RR Lyrae stars are horizontal branch giants that pulsate with periods of 0.2–1 day.
They have nearly constant absolute magnitude, making them excellent standard candles.
They are used to measure distances within the Milky Way and to nearby galaxies.
RR Lyrae stars are metal-poor population II stars found in globular clusters.
They are named after the prototype RR Lyrae in Lyra.

Delta Cephei.explanation: Delta Cephei is the prototype of Cepheid variable stars crucial for measuring distances
points: Delta Cephei is a yellow supergiant that pulsates with a period of 5.366 days.
Cepheids have a period-luminosity relationship discovered by Henrietta Leavitt.
This relationship makes them fundamental for cosmic distance ladder.
Delta Cephei varies from magnitude +3.5 to +4.4.
It is the prototype of classical Cepheids used to measure distances to nearby galaxies.

Beta Lyrae.explanation: Beta Lyrae is a contact binary where two stars are so close they share their outer atmosphere
points: Beta Lyrae is an eclipsing contact binary with a period of 12.9 days.
The two stars are B-type giants that overflow their Roche lobes.
Material streams from the secondary to the primary, forming an accretion disk.
It is the prototype of Beta Lyrae-type binaries.
The system is highly variable due to changing geometry and mass transfer.

Algol.explanation: Algol the Demon Star is an eclipsing binary that dims every 2.87 days
points: Algol (Beta Persei) is an eclipsing binary with a period of 2.87 days.
The primary is a B8V star; the secondary is a K0 subgiant.
The secondary fills its Roche lobe and transfers mass to the primary.
Algol dims from magnitude +2.1 to +3.4 during eclipses.
It was one of the first variable stars recognized (1667) and is called the 'Demon Star'.

W Ursae Majoris.explanation: W UMa is a contact binary where two stars are touching and share common envelopes
points: W Ursae Majoris is the prototype of W UMa-type contact binaries.
The two stars share a common envelope and have nearly equal temperatures.
They have very short periods (0.3–1 day) and continuous variation.
Mass ratios are typically close to 1.
They are common in the galaxy and represent a late stage of binary evolution.

AM Canum Venaticorum.explanation: AM CVn is an ultra-compact binary where white dwarf pulls helium from another star
points: AM CVn stars are helium-rich cataclysmic variables with very short periods (5–65 minutes).
They consist of a white dwarf accreting helium from a companion.
They are progenitors of Type Ia supernovae or other explosive events.
AM CVn is the prototype of this rare class.
They emit strongly in ultraviolet and X-rays.

Pulsars.explanation: Pulsars are spinning neutron stars that emit beams of radio waves like a cosmic lighthouse
points: Pulsars are rapidly rotating neutron stars with strong magnetic fields.
They emit beams of radiation from their magnetic poles that sweep past Earth.
The first pulsar (PSR B1919+21) was discovered in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell Burnell.
Millisecond pulsars are extremely stable and used as cosmic clocks.
Some pulsars emit across the electromagnetic spectrum, including X-rays and gamma rays.

Magnetar.explanation: Magnetars have magnetic fields a quadrillion times stronger than Earth's
points: Magnetars are neutron stars with magnetic fields of 10^14 to 10^15 Gauss.
Their fields power soft gamma repeaters and anomalous X-ray pulsars.
Magnetar outbursts can release enormous energy in seconds.
Their fields decay rapidly compared to normal pulsars.
They are among the most magnetic objects known in the universe.

Neutron Star.explanation: Neutron stars are incredibly dense collapsed stars where a teaspoon would weigh a billion tons
points: Neutron stars have masses 1.4–2 solar masses compressed into a ~10–20 km radius.
They are supported by neutron degeneracy pressure.
Surface gravity is billions of times Earth's.
They have extremely strong magnetic fields (10^8–10^15 Gauss).
They form from the core collapse of massive stars in supernova explosions.

White Dwarf.explanation: White dwarfs are the dead cores of stars like our Sun that will slowly cool over billions of years
points: White dwarfs have masses up to about 1.4 solar masses (Chandrasekhar limit) but are Earth-sized.
They are supported by electron degeneracy pressure.
They slowly cool and fade over billions of years, eventually becoming black dwarfs.
Many have strong magnetic fields and some are rapidly rotating pulsars.
They are the final stage for most stars (including the Sun).

Black Dwarf.explanation: Black dwarfs are theoretical cooled white dwarfs but none exist yet as the universe is too young
points: Black dwarfs would be cold, dark remnants of white dwarfs after they cool completely.
Cooling time exceeds the current age of the universe (~13.8 billion years).
They would have temperatures near absolute zero and be barely detectable.
They represent the final stage of low- to medium-mass stellar evolution.
The universe is currently too young for any black dwarfs to exist.

Brown Dwarf.explanation: Brown dwarfs are failed stars too small to sustain hydrogen fusion in their cores
points: Brown dwarfs have masses between 13 and 80 Jupiter masses.
They can briefly fuse deuterium but not hydrogen.
They cool over time and eventually resemble giant planets.
Some have methane in their atmospheres and are classified as Y dwarfs.
They bridge the gap between planets and stars.

Red Dwarf.explanation: Red dwarfs are the smallest and most common stars in the universe and can live for trillions of years
points: Red dwarfs are M-type main-sequence stars with masses 0.08–0.6 solar masses.
They are fully convective and burn hydrogen very slowly.
Their lifetimes can exceed the current age of the universe by orders of magnitude.
Most nearby stars are red dwarfs (Proxima Centauri, Barnard's Star).
They often have strong flares and can strip planetary atmospheres.

Yellow Dwarf.explanation: Yellow dwarfs like our Sun are medium-sized stable stars that live for about 10 billion years
points: Yellow dwarfs are G-type main-sequence stars with masses 0.8–1.2 solar masses.
They have surface temperatures of 5,300–6,000 K and are stable hydrogen burners.
The Sun is a typical G2V yellow dwarf.
They are common and long-lived enough to host complex life.
They eventually evolve into red giants and white dwarfs.

Blue Giant.explanation: Blue giants are massive hot stars that live fast and die young in huge supernova explosions
points: Blue giants are O and B-type stars with masses 2–150+ solar masses.
They have surface temperatures of 10,000–50,000 K and are extremely luminous.
They have short main-sequence lifetimes (millions of years).
They end their lives in core-collapse supernovae.
Examples include Rigel, Spica, and most stars in young clusters.

Red Giant.explanation: Red giants are aging stars that expand enormously as they burn the last of their hydrogen
points: Red giants have exhausted core hydrogen and now fuse helium or shell hydrogen.
They expand to 10–100+ times their original radius.
They are luminous but cool (3,500–4,500 K) with red-orange colors.
They lose mass through strong stellar winds.
They are a transitional phase before becoming white dwarfs or exploding.

Hypergiant.explanation: Hypergiants are the rarest and most extreme class of stars with enormous mass and luminosity
points: Hypergiants have luminosities of 100,000–5,000,000 solar luminosities.
They are massive stars (20–150+ solar masses) in late evolutionary stages.
They are extremely unstable and lose mass rapidly.
Examples include Rho Cassiopeiae, VY Canis Majoris, and Pistol Star.
They are among the most luminous and rarest stars in galaxies.

Protostar.explanation: Protostars are forming stars hidden in dense clouds of gas and dust before ignition
points: Protostars form from collapsing molecular cloud cores.
They are surrounded by accretion disks and envelopes.
They are not yet fusing hydrogen and are powered by gravitational contraction.
They are observed primarily in infrared due to dust obscuration.
Protostellar phase lasts about 10^5–10^6 years.

T Tauri.explanation: T Tauri stars are very young unstable stars just beginning the process of nuclear fusion
points: T Tauri stars are pre-main-sequence stars with masses 0.5–2 solar masses.
They are highly variable due to accretion and magnetic activity.
They have strong stellar winds and bipolar outflows.
Many have protoplanetary disks (proplyds).
They are found in star-forming regions like Orion Nebula.

Herbig Ae/Be.explanation: Herbig Ae/Be stars are young intermediate-mass stars with disks of material still forming
points: Herbig Ae/Be stars are pre-main-sequence stars with masses 2–8 solar masses.
They have circumstellar disks and strong emission lines.
They are surrounded by reflection nebulae.
They bridge the gap between T Tauri and massive star formation.
They often show UXOR-type variability.

Subdwarf.explanation: Subdwarf stars are small dim stars fusing helium rather than the usual hydrogen
points: Subdwarfs are metal-poor Population II stars.
They lie below the main sequence due to lower metallicity.
They have higher surface gravity and bluer colors.
They are older stars with different evolutionary paths.
They are important for understanding galactic evolution.

Subgiant.explanation: Subgiant stars are just beginning the transition from main sequence to red giant phase
points: Subgiants have exhausted core hydrogen but not yet started shell burning significantly.
They are brighter and larger than main-sequence stars of the same temperature.
They are in a brief evolutionary phase.
Examples include Procyon A and some stars in open clusters.
They are useful for studying stellar evolution.

Wolf-Rayet.explanation: Wolf-Rayet stars shed their outer layers in fierce stellar winds exposing their hot cores
points: Wolf-Rayet stars are massive, evolved stars with strong stellar winds.
They have lost their hydrogen envelopes, exposing CNO-processed material.
They have surface temperatures of 20,000–210,000 K.
They are very luminous and have strong emission lines.
They are progenitors of Type Ib/c supernovae and gamma-ray bursts.

Carbon Star.explanation: Carbon stars have so much carbon in their atmosphere that soot-like compounds form
points: Carbon stars are red giants with C/O ratio > 1.
They have strong carbon molecular bands (C2, CN).
They produce heavy elements through the s-process.
They are surrounded by carbon-rich circumstellar shells.
They are important sources of carbon in the galaxy.

Technetium Star.explanation: Technetium stars contain unstable radioactive technetium showing active nucleosynthesis
points: Technetium stars show technetium-99 lines in their spectra.
Technetium has no stable isotopes and decays quickly.
Its presence indicates recent s-process nucleosynthesis.
Most are asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars.
They provide direct evidence of stellar nucleosynthesis.

Lithium Star.explanation: Lithium-rich giant stars are a puzzle as normal giants should destroy their lithium not keep it
points: Lithium-rich giants have lithium abundances 10–1000 times higher than expected.
Standard stellar evolution predicts lithium depletion.
Possible mechanisms include planet engulfment or unusual mixing.
They are rare and still poorly understood.
They provide clues to non-standard stellar processes.

Barium Star.explanation: Barium stars have anomalously high amounts of heavy elements from a companion star
points: Barium stars show strong barium and s-process element lines.
They are typically giants with white dwarf companions.
Material rich in s-process elements was transferred from the companion.
They are important for studying binary evolution and nucleosynthesis.
Many are CH or CH-like stars.

Ap Star.explanation: Ap stars have abnormal amounts of certain elements and extremely strong magnetic fields
points: Ap stars are chemically peculiar A-type stars with strong magnetic fields.
They show overabundances of Sr, Cr, Eu, and rare earths.
Fields range from hundreds to tens of thousands of Gauss.
Elements are stratified in their atmospheres.
They are slow rotators with strong magnetic braking.

FK Comae.explanation: FK Comae type stars are rapidly spinning giants with extreme star spot activity
points: FK Com stars are rapidly rotating G/K giants.
They show strong chromospheric activity and starspots.
They may be the result of binary mergers.
They have very short rotation periods (days).
They are extreme examples of magnetic activity.

Flare Star.explanation: Flare stars are red dwarfs that produce powerful sudden flares brightening dramatically
points: Flare stars are M-type dwarfs with strong magnetic activity.
They can increase brightness by factors of 10–100 in minutes.
Flares emit across UV, X-ray, and radio wavelengths.
They can affect planetary habitability.
Examples include Proxima Centauri and AD Leonis.

BY Draconis.explanation: BY Draconis stars vary in brightness due to large dark star spots on their surface
points: BY Dra stars are spotted M-type dwarfs with rotation-induced variability.
They show quasi-periodic brightness changes due to starspots.
They are young and magnetically active.
They are the prototype of spotted flare stars.
They provide insights into stellar magnetism.

FU Orionis.explanation: FU Orionis stars are young stars that suddenly brighten 100 fold due to disk accretion
points: FUors are pre-main-sequence stars with dramatic luminosity increases.
Brightening is caused by increased accretion from a circumstellar disk.
They can stay bright for decades to centuries.
They are rare and important for understanding disk accretion.
FU Orionis is the prototype of this class.

EX Lupi.explanation: EX Lupi stars are young stars with episodic outbursts caused by instabilities in their disk
points: EXors are pre-main-sequence stars with recurrent outbursts.
Outbursts are less extreme than FUors but more frequent.
They are caused by disk instabilities or accretion events.
EX Lupi is the prototype.
They help study episodic accretion.

Symbiotic Star.explanation: Symbiotic stars are binary systems with a red giant and white dwarf interacting closely
points: Symbiotic stars have a red giant transferring mass to a white dwarf.
They show emission lines from ionized nebula.
Some undergo nova-like outbursts.
They are important for understanding binary evolution.
They are rare and often variable.

Cataclysmic Variable.explanation: Cataclysmic variables are binaries where a white dwarf pulls material from a companion
points: CVs consist of a white dwarf accreting from a main-sequence or giant companion.
They show outbursts (novae, dwarf novae) due to accretion disk instabilities.
They are important for understanding accretion physics.
Many have strong magnetic fields.
They are common in the galaxy.

Nova.explanation: A nova occurs when a white dwarf accretes enough material to trigger a thermonuclear explosion
points: Novae are surface explosions on white dwarfs in binary systems.
They increase brightness by 10–15 magnitudes.
They are not destructive to the white dwarf.
They recur in some systems (recurrent novae).
They synthesize some heavy elements.

Supernova.explanation: A supernova explosion releases as much energy as the Sun will emit in its entire lifetime
points: Supernovae are catastrophic explosions marking the death of massive stars or white dwarfs.
Type Ia from white dwarf detonation; Type II from core collapse.
They synthesize and disperse heavy elements.
They can outshine entire galaxies briefly.
They leave behind neutron stars or black holes.

Hypernova.explanation: Hypernovae are incredibly powerful supernovae that may produce long gamma-ray bursts
points: Hypernovae are extreme core-collapse supernovae with energies 10–100 times normal SN.
They are associated with long GRBs.
They involve very massive, rapidly rotating stars.
They produce large amounts of nickel and other heavy elements.
They are rare and extremely energetic.

Kilonova.explanation: Kilonovae occur when two neutron stars collide creating all heavy elements like gold
points: Kilonovae are electromagnetic counterparts to neutron star mergers.
They are powered by r-process nucleosynthesis.
They produce heavy elements including gold and uranium.
They are fast and fade quickly.
GW170817 was the first observed kilonova.

Quasar.explanation: Quasars are the most luminous objects in the universe powered by supermassive black holes
points: Quasars are active galactic nuclei with supermassive black holes accreting matter.
They can outshine their host galaxies by factors of 100–1000.
They are seen at great distances (high redshift).
They are powered by accretion disks and relativistic jets.
They are important for understanding galaxy evolution.

Blazar.explanation: Blazars are quasars with a jet of material aimed directly at Earth
points: Blazars are AGN with relativistic jets pointed nearly at the observer.
They show strong variability across wavelengths.
They emit gamma rays and can be highly polarized.
They are the most extreme class of AGN.
They are important for studying relativistic jets.

Seyfert Galaxy Core.explanation: Seyfert galaxies have active galactic nuclei with bright cores visible at multiple wavelengths
points: Seyfert galaxies are spiral galaxies with active nuclei.
They have bright, point-like cores.
Type 1 have broad emission lines; Type 2 have narrow lines.
They are lower luminosity than quasars.
They are common nearby AGN.

Microquasar.explanation: Microquasars are stellar-mass black holes that mimic quasar behavior on a smaller scale
points: Microquasars are X-ray binaries with relativistic jets.
They have black holes of 5–20 solar masses.
They show jet ejections and superluminal motion.
They are important for studying accretion and jet physics.
They are galactic analogs of quasars.

Black Hole.explanation: Black holes have gravity so strong that nothing not even light can escape from them
points: Black holes form from the collapse of massive stars or mergers.
They have an event horizon beyond which nothing can escape.
Stellar-mass black holes are 3–100 solar masses.
Supermassive black holes are millions to billions of solar masses.
They are detected via gravitational effects and accretion disks.

Sagittarius A*.explanation: Sagittarius A* is the supermassive black hole at the center of our Milky Way galaxy
points: Sagittarius A* has a mass of about 4.3 million solar masses.
It is located about 26,000 light-years from Earth.
It was imaged by the Event Horizon Telescope in 2022.
It is relatively quiet compared to other supermassive black holes.
It is orbited by stars used to measure its mass.

TON 618.explanation: TON 618 is one of the most massive black holes known with 66 billion solar masses
points: TON 618 is a hyperluminous quasar powered by a 66 billion solar mass black hole.
It is one of the most massive known black holes.
It is located about 10.4 billion light-years away.
It outshines most galaxies.
It is an extreme example of early universe black hole growth.
